These permits would be more properly termed "letters of admission." The letters of admission were to bring in the relatives of persons already in Canada, and their entry was subject entirely to the approval of the department.
The second point that I think I should call to the attention of the house relates to the number of so-called permits credited to each person. More properly the return should have been divided into the number of permits and the number of persons included in those permits. For instance, an individual who obtained three letters of admission might bring in eleven persons. He is credited with obtaining eleven permits, when as a matter of fact he obtained only three. Several hon. members have spoken to me about this, and I think it is only fair that the public at least should have a correct impression of what the return means.

Marine-life saving service, including rewards for saving life, $80,000.

I wish to direct the attention of the house to a disaster that overtook shipping on the great lakes last fall, and to another disaster that occurred on lake Erie a month ago. Only a miserable $8,000 out of this vote is provided for the great lakes to safeguard the interests of 5,000 seamen, who are exposed to very grave danger during the months of October, November, December and January. These men are engaged in carrying the grain crop of Canada on the great lakes and although operating Canadian vessels, they have to trust to the mercy of an American life saving station in the event of accident. This is not creditable to Canada. On the great lakes we have a life saving system which is nothing but a relic of the days before confederation. That is all it is. You can spend millions of dollars on railways and canals but only $80,000 in life saving, and only a miserable proportion of that on the great lakes. I wish to protest on behalf' of these brave seamen who are left to the mercy of Americans when they are in danger. There is nof an icebreaker to help these men or a decent life-saving station on the great lakes except the one at Toronto maintained by the local taxpayers.
There are ten Liberals in this house representing Ontario and maritime seats; only two or three of them are present to-day to speak for their constituencies. Where are these gentlemen who represent maritime cities around lake Superior, Georgian bay, lake Huron and lake Erie? Canada is proud to call herself a nation and yet in time of disaster these brave seamen are left, I repeat, without any help at all. We are thinking more of trade than we are of human life. Something should be done by this government to safeguard the lives of these men, but instead of that all the government is voting for their protection on the great lakes is a miserly $8,000. The government can afford millions of dollars for breakwaters and wharves and other material things, but not a dollar to protect these men, blood brothers of the men who fought at St. Julien, and scaled the heights of Passchendale. The hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa) talks a lot of nonsense about equality of status. I do not see the hon. gentleman in his place this afternoon, but if

Supply-Marine and Fisheries
he would spend more of his time in an endeavour to solve economic problems and to promote the welfare of these brave men it would be far better than all the academic talk we hear from him in season and out of season. What does he care about these sailors? He talks about nationalism. It is a sham nationalism; that is all it is. If we had a .proper spirit of nationalism we would do something to protect these brave men who night and day are doing their utmost to advance the prosperity of the country. Many of these men who serve as seamen on the great lakes, transporting our grain, have applied to the government for consideration, and in this regard I have a huge pile of papers brought down as a return to an order regarding this question and asking for relief. In addition to this I myself appeared before the minister with a deputation of lake mariners and the Masters and Mates Association, the year before last and the year before that asking that something be done for these men. This country is following a pennywise-pound-foolish policy-spending millions of dollars on breakwaters, wharves and the like and absolutely neglecting these poor men.
It is the duty of the government to protect the lives of its citizens whether on the great lakes or on the ocean, but what is this government doing? All they have is a little bit of a life-saving boat on the great lakes. There are no stations at Port Dalhousie or at Hamilton; the oity of Toronto spends $60,000 of the taxpayers' money to protect the shipping on lake Ontario, and that life-saving crew has been called to Muskoka, to Georgian bay, to lake Huron, to lake Erie and to the Niagara river. On behalf of the taxpayers of the city of Toronto I wish to protest against this .added responsibility to their already heavy burden. If there is a disaster on these lakes what does the department do? A wreck commissioner is sent for, a man who knows something about salt water but who knows little or nothing about the great lakes, and he holds an inquiry. The wreck may have been the fault of the owners of the ship; it may have been caused by the fact that the captain did not have proper assistance, but the wreck commissioner comes along and takes away the captain's license, putting him out of a position and preventing him from earning his living. Canada has a government at Ottawa which chatters about our new status but which does nothing to help the poor sailors. Some years ago a parliamentary inquiry was held in England, and it was determined among other things that each ship must have a Plimsoll mark on the hull, but so far as shipping is concerned Canadla is still a colony. There are ten members in this house whose constituencies border on these great inland waters; I refer to the hon. member for East Lambton (Mr. Fansher), the hon. member for West Lambton (Mr. Goodison), the hon. member for North Huron (Mr. Spotton), the hon. member for South Huron (Mr. McMillan), the hon. member for East Essex (Mr. Odette), the hon. member for North Bruce (Mr. Malcolm), the hon. member for South Bruce (Mr. Hall), the hon. member for North Grey (Mr. Telford), the hon. member for Southeast Grey (Miss Macphail) and the hon. member for East Algoma (Mr. Bowman). With the exception of one, these ten members support the Liberal government, yet we do nothing in this regard.
The government should vote a large sum of money for this work; we should have proper ice crushers and other equipment. They have this equipment on the St. Lawrence river and in the gulf, and modern aids to navigation, but apparently these upper lakes are to be left unprotected during the early winter and fall storms. The canals are open until early in December, yet our sailors on the great lakes are left to the kindness of the Americans if life-saving assistance is needed. The Department of Marine and Fisheries should be up and doing something, instead of spending all this money in the lower St. Lawrence. In one particular disaster which took place on the great lakes more lives were lost than in the battle of Queenston Heights in 1812, yet all this parliament does is to spend a large part of its time discussing academic questions. I am surprised that my hon. friends to the left, who have done a great deal of good work in connection with questions respecting public rights, do not take some action in this regard, since these sailors play an important part in advancing one of our great basic industries and in keeping trade in Canadian channels.
What is the situation in the United States? The War department has a life-saving station at the port of Buffalo consisting of 250 men, who go out over lake Erie in that district to protect the millions of people travelling up and down in the large steamers. They have other stations at Erie, at Cleveland, at Toledo and at Detroit; all along the lakes they have companies of naval reservists, some of them composed of as many as 300 and 400 men and assisted also by volunteer reserves. They are on the lookout all the time; they have a wireless system, aids to navigation, they have up-to-date fast boats, and in many cases they have on the upper lakes large ice crushers with which to assist these brave men

Supply-Marine and Fisheries
instead of leaving them ait the mercy of tlhe graves and fall storms.
I wish to protest against this condition on behalf of the lake sailors' associations, and the Masters' and Mates' Association; ever since I have been in parliament these men have been coming to Ottawa with memoranda in connection with this matter, only to have their data filed away in cold storage. It is all very well to say that $80,000 is 'being spent in this service, but nothing has been done on the great lakes; large numbers of Canadian boats are lying idle in Canadian ports while American hulls are carrying the grain of this country. In addition to that, these captains have many other grievances arising out of the lack of aids to navigation such as lighthouses, beacon lights, wireless apparatus, and many other things of that kind. AM the money has been spent in the lower 3t. Lawrence, and I protest on behalf of the taxpayers of Ontario, who pay 42 per cent rf the taxes of Canada.
I have brought up this question for four or five sessions of parliament without being able to accomplish anything. There should be one or two large life-saving stations on lake Superior; one should be located at Port Arthur, Fort William and the Soo. The hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Manion) is not afraid or too proud to fight for his constituents or for the people in other parts of the country; some day he will have a great port at the bead of the lakes, but there is no sign of a proper life-saving station being located there, with ice crushers, wireless equipment and the other necessary aids to navigation. If there are to be no life-saving stations let the minister declare that after November 15 or to December 10 no more grain shall be carried, but if the men are to be sent out on the great lakes in the storms which prevail during late fall, they are entitled to all the protection and assistance it is possible to give.
No doubt the minister will get up and say that nothing can be done, that we are spending all we can or as much as the previous government did. This is an example of the way these estimates are considered. We only hold post mortems on the estimates; a great deal of the money has been spent by the time we come to consider them. I venture to say that if we held a parliamentary inquiry into this question many members would be horrified to find the true state of affairs on the great lakes. The man who has some freight to be carried will charter an American hull rather than a Canadian boat because he knows he can get a better insurance rate when

the insurance company learns that the boat will have the life-saving protection afforded by the United States government in the bad weather of November and December. In the dangerous waters of lake Superior, Georgian bay and lake Huron there is no life-saving equipment.
There is a large sand shoal off the Niagara river, and the attention of the minister has been called to it many times. What is the government going to do about it? Are they going to wait until one of these large boats founder with two or three thousand people aboard and have the disasters of the upper lakes occurring also in lake Ontario? I wish the Minister of Labour (Mr. Heenan) were here to tell us something about deep-sea diving, and what it feels like to go down to the bottom of the sea. But he is over in Europe now trying to pacify that country, and I see he is riding around in aeroplanes. He represents one of these maritime constituencies on the upper lakes, adjacent to the scene of one of these disasters and he could tell of the necessity of getting something done.
Petitions have been sent to the government but they are doing nothing, and they will do nothing as long as there is an opposition to put up with it. I am going to move, as a censure of the government, that the item be reduced. It is the only weapon I have in committee. I do not wish to delay the house by moving an amendment to the motion to go into supply, but will simply move that this vote be reduced in committee although I would like to see the vote half a million.
If we had a great lake disaster it would wake up the whole country, and as a member of the opposition, representing a maritime constituency, I wish to protest against the continuance of the present indifference and neglect. I protest against the taxpayers of the city of Toronto having to expend about $60,000 to maintain a life-saving department for the whole lake when the government fails. They are called to Port Dalhousie, Hamilton, Georgian bay, the Muskoka lakes; they went to the Moon river to drag for five or six boys who were drowned there. They go all over the lakes, simply because we have a so-called Liberal government that will not make the expenditure to protect these brave men on the lakes.
As I say, I do not wish to take up the time of the house, but I am going to move that this item be reduced by $15,000, as a censure of the government for the lax way it has treated these brave men on the lakes. I, therefore, move as follows:
That item No. 211 be reduced from $80,000 to $65,000.

Supply-Marine and Fisheries

As one of the Liberal-
Conservative members from a maritime con-stituencj'' bordering on lake Huron, where many a home is mourning for the loved ones who have found a watery grave in lake Huron and the other lakes, I wish to say "amen" to everything the hon. member for Toronto Northwest (Mr. Church) has said. Mr. Chairman, I am utterly amazed that the Prime Minister of Canada and his colleagues in the cabinet not only lend an unsympathetic ear, but entirely disregard, the pleadings we have heard1 this afternoon. Only one member of the government, the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Malcolm), who comes from a neighbouring county, has given any attention whatever to these remarks. We are accustomed to read and hear the Prime Minister's speeches where he says in almost every paragraph that he wants this house and "the country" to understand so-and-so. His efforts and remarks are all to the country. I have never known of such a self-centred and selfsatisfied bunch of men in my life as the present administration. They have drunk deep of all kinds of knowledge and they apparently cannot learn anything from any private member who may rise in his seat.
It is only a short time ago that they showed great concern for the people residing in the vicinity of these lakes. I am not going to take up the time of the house further than just to say "amen" to everything the hon. member for Toronto Northwest has said, regarding some effort being made to protect the lives of the brave boys from my county and neighbouring counties who traverse the lakes and keep open these great arteries of trade and commerce. I would like the house and the country, and the men who have shed and will shed tears again, when addressing citizens of Canada to understand that these pleadings have been entirely disregarded by the members of the government, with the exception of the Minister of Trade and Commerce. I want the people in my county and the neighbouring counties to understand that it has been practically a joke, so far as the present administration is concerned, and if they want any relief I suppose the only thing to do is to change the complexion of the administration.

I have no hesitation in
saying that I sympathize most heartily with the representations which have been made by the two previous speakers. If we are not doing more than we are doing at the present time, it is not on account of a lack of sympathy or consideration for these navigators on the great lakes. This vote is put througti year after year. It started long ago when the boats navigating the great lakes were not
what they are to-day, and the life-saving service was established to cope with that situation. But with the great developments which have taken place regarding navigation on the great lakes, it is impossible to cope with the situation with the very limited amount which is voted year by year. With the sum we are asking for this year, we could not prevent such accidents as the hon. member has just referred to.
It must be remembered that the majority of the accidents which do occur on the groat lakes happen towards the close of the navigation season, and the navigators themselves and the proprietors of the ship take a certain amount of risk in running their boats at this late period of the year. It would help very materially if some sort of an understanding were arrived at between the shipping interests whereby navigation would cease when it was not considered to be safe on the lakes. It would be impossible to stop all the accidents which occur on the lakes. We are doing the best we can with the votes we are getting, but I am free to admit that we could do more if we had a little more money. But even if we spent double the amount we are asking for this year, we could not cope with the situation.
Reference has been made to the United States, it being claimed that they have a more adequate system. As far as the number of accidents is concerned, I think we compare very favourably with the United States. They have had as many accidents as we have had in Canada on the great lakes or anywhere else, and to say that we should provide lifesaving stations and life-saving apparatus at every point where there is navigation, or where there is dianger, would mean that we would have to come to parliament and ask for several millions of dollars. We would need that amount to cope with all the representations made by certain gentlemen. We are in sympathy with those who sail the lakes, and we sympathize with the families who have lost loved ones, .but we must admit that with the best system possible we will never be in a position to prevent all accidents and casualties in navigation.
I cannot agree with my hon. friend when he asks us to reduce the item. If we are not doing enough with the appropriation of $80,000 that we have at present, we shall certainly do much less if we reduce this small appropriation. Good service has been rendered by the small stations that we have, with their limited means and apparatus, and it would be a mistake to do away with them even if they are not as effective as they would be if we were spending millions instead of thousands of dollars as we are doing now. I might express the view of the officers of the department, after

Supply-Marine and Fisheries
having studied the matter. They are of opinion that it is almost impossible to cope entirely with the situation which has been revealed and the prevention of accidents. The technical men of the department are of the view that the best safeguards in regard to navigation and shipping are those which they have enumerated in a short memorandum which has been given to me, as follows:
1.	By the provision and maintenance of modern aids to navigation, including accurate and reliable charts and sailing directions.
2.	By providing that all vessels shall be properly equipped with lifesaving apparatus.
3.	By providing that only certified and fully qualified officers shall be employed in the navigation of vessels.
i. By the dissemination by radio broadcast and by the display of land signals of information relating to conditions of navigation, weather conditions generally and particularly of impending storms.
I may add to that that the regulations in regard to seaworthiness of vessels are applied most strictly. If we could apply in practice all these suggestions, we would help to solve the problem and give valuable assistance to the shipping interests. Indeed, if all these suggestions were put into practice and accepted with good will on the part of the shipping interests, we would do more than we could ever do by maintaining or developing the lifesaving system that we have at the present time. Personally I would not object to spending a larger amount of money on a bigger scheme for life-having; I admit it is worth the money that we might spend on it; but we are not quite sure whether we would be in a position even then to cope with the situation as it exists. My sentiments in the matter are just as good and strong as those of the 'hon. member for Toronto Northwest (Mr. Church) and the hon. member for North Huron (Mr. Spotton) who has just taken his seat. We are ready to do everything we can for the safety of the mariners and up to the present time with the limited means and ap.-propriation granted to us we have done pretty well even in comparison with what has been done in the United States. We ought to retain this appropriation. If we do little, let us do what we are doing at present and do not let us do away with the existing services which have proved, generally speaking, their efficiency and benefit to navigators.

This amendment is the
only weapon I have. I would be willing to withdraw the amendment if the minister would increase the appropriation to half a million dollars, but I object to the minister telling the committee that his system compares favourably with that of the United States. The department have not enough life-saving 
stations on the great lakes. They have only small lifeboats at Cobourg, Goderich, Pelee Point, Port Stanley and so forth. These boats cannot go out to a ship at all owing to the waves raised by the storms. I have seen these small boats at the stations on the lakes and they are little life. boats, that cannot get out of the port in a storm. How are they going to get out in the month of December? I am sorry I have not with me a couple of hundred pictures that I have of disasters on the upper lakes. I have one here which shows the ice on the great lakes when our brave sailors were out there battling with the storm. The minister has not an up-to-date life-saving station on the entire great lakes; he has to protect these men who are carrying our grain on the great lakes, only a few lifeboats like those that are found on the top of a big vessel. I have here a picture of a tug at Owen Sound. It could not get out at all. This is a picture of a freighter covered up to the third deck with ice. A little rowboat cannot deal with a situation like that. It is almost comparable with the government's contemptible little navy in time of war. I have visited the life-saving stations at Detroit and Buffalo. They have a company of 250 naval reservists stationed at Buffalo, Detroit, and up the lakes, and in the summer time they have a volunteer company ready to go round the lakes when called upon and to give help if necessary. It was due to these United States men alone that our men were rescued. Just last month a disaster happened at Port Dover and they had to wait for a week to get a life-saving tug from Bessemer or Erie, Pennsylvania, to come to the rescue. Hon. Forbes Godfrey wired Hon. J. S. Martin, Minister of Agriculture, congratulating him on having got the United States life tug; and in seven days the men were brought into Port Dover.
I contend that this item ought to be increased to more than a million dollars for proper lifesaving stations to help the grain trade on the great lakes and to protect the travelling public and sailors. Are we to be at the mercy of American life-saving stations for our protection on the great lakes? More than 5,000 sailors are left at the mercy of the few small boats and there is not a modem, up-to-date station except the one at Toronto which :s maintained by the taxpayers of that city at a cost of $60,000 a year. The government should have ice-breaking tugs., modern marine equipment, wireless, fast tugs, lighthouses, sirens and other modem aids to navigation on the great lakes, the same as they have on the St. Lawrence and down in the gulf. A sum of $80,000 is not sufficient to

Supply-*Marine and Fisheries
establish one station. The department could not secure a proper tug for that amount. Such boats would cost as much as $100,000. Why does the Department of Marine and Fisheries not borrow some of the ships of the merchant marine which cost from a million to a million and a half dollars and which were sold for $50,000? They could have been converted into proper tugs to handle the situation on the great lakes. To-day it cannot be handled at all, and nothing will be done by the department. I do not really intend that $16,000 should be struck off this item, but an amendment of this kind is the only weapon I have in committee of supply. I could have brought up the subject on the motion to go into supply but I did not wish to delay the business of the house. I think it would be a good thing for the taxpayers if the session were closed up to-night before the government bring down any more supplementary estimates running into eight or ten million dollars. The Department of Marine and Fisheries is incapable of doing anything in regard to taking care of the situation on the great lakes. Until some members of parliament and government officials happen to be on some of these boats in a storm on the great lakes nothing will be done and the department will continue having little bits of rowboats at Cobourg, Goderich and other places and such contemptible small boats to rescue lives.
An hon. member from one of the Essex constituencies called attention to this matter a year ago in the house when there was a debate on this very item. The week after, at Pelee island, three or four men were drowned owing to the fact that there was no life-saving station there. Since then a station has been installed, but what is the use of a station and of a small life-boat on a stormy December night, with high seas running? I had a report-I am sorry I have not got it here-[DOT] showing what the United States government is doing in the matter of life-saving in its various harbours and ports. They have organized a permanent life-saving corps. At the city of Detroit, for instance, there is a corps of over two hundred men, and a lifesaving station at the Detroit Boat Club. They have also naval ships right at the port and and all along the river ready to go out on the lakes to the rescue of any large passenger boats that may be in distress. All we have is a life-saving boat about the length of a row boat and about as long as this table. Talk about $80,000! That is not nearly enough to spend on this vitally important work of life-saving. I have been down to Ottawa with the marine association representatives and with lake captains, and I know that they are left at the mercy of the politicians. Talk about Liberalism! There is no Liberalism at all in this country to-day. We have on the government benches the most moss-backed form of Toryism that there ever was in the history of the world. We have a government that lets these men drown in the lake storms. I withdrew my amendment, but I shall consult with the leader of our party with a view to moving an amendment on the motion to go into supply, because I should like a vote taken on the principle whether or not these men working on the lakes are entitled to protection.

I think there is much to be said in favour of the position that has been taken by my hon. friend who has moved the amendment, but I think that under all the circumstances he will be wise in withdrawing the amendment on the present occasion. An amendment to reduce the amount which has been placed in the main estimates for the purpose of life-saving would, I think, be probably misunderstood in the country, because the real object of the hon. member is to increase that amount, not to reduce it.
I must say, having regard to the situation on the great lake3, that the sum of SSO.OOO appearing in the estimates for the purpose of life-saving throughout the whole Dominion of Canada seems exceedingly small. I understand that at places like Goderich and Southampton on lake Huron, there is only an allotment of some $300, and that for the Georgian bay waters there is no allotment whatever. We. all know that scarcely a season passes without some serious misfortune occurring, involving loss of life in the waters which comprise our great lakes system. The amounts which we now vote are entirely inadequate for the purpose for which we are voting them. When one looks at the estimates and finds that we can afford to vote annually for topographical surveys, $400,000 odd, for geodetic surveys, $265,000, for geological surveys, $205,000, and so on, surely we should be able to afford in this country a very much larger sum than $80,000 for the purpose of life-saving, and I think the minister would do well before this house meets again to reconsider this whole question. The money which he spends now in many of these places is practically wasted money; it is of no avail in case of accident. The $300 at Goderich, the $300 at Southampton, the $300 at Cobourg, is practically a worthless expenditure. I do not advooate any tremendous or unwarranted expenditure in this respeyt, but I think that the minister and the government

Supply-Marine and Fisheries
would do well before the house meets again next year to see that there is appropriated an amount that will be commensurate with the [DOT]difficulties which we have always to face in the autumn on these waters.

I do not seek a reduction
in this vote. What I do seek is more efficient service and dispatch from some of the life-saving stations that we have. I refer particularly to the Point Pelee life-saving station. WThen the committee rose last evening, the hon. member for West Essex (Mr. Robinson) had spoken of the liife-savingi station at Point Pelee, and my reference was to the southeast shoal lighthouse. I think the minister misunderstood my question at the time, I hope to have an opportunity to deal with the matter which I started to take up last night under these estimates, and I propose now to bring to the attention of the minister the most deplorable conditions that exist at Point Pelee life-saving station.
During the last session of the house I put a number of questions on the order paper, some twenty-five in number, in connection with the operation of the Point Pelee lifesaving station. One was:
What was the total cost for maintaining the station for the year 1926?
The answer to that question was:
$7,378.76. (Up to date for fiscal year 1926-27) (Covers wages, board, repairs and labour supplies, clothing, and so forth.)
Another question I asked was:
When was the station first established?
I also asked:
14. What has been the cost of maintenance: (a) total cost; (b) each year since it was established?
_ 15. What training or practice is participated in by the crew under the present coxswain?
The answer to question 15 was:
Drills performed twice a week. (Include managing the lifeboat and other duties connected with the station and an exercise of four or five miles in the boat.)
The cost of maintaining this life-saving station has risen each year. In 1903 the cost was $730; in 1911, $1,838.25; 1912, $4,125.97; 1916, $10,626.26; which included $5,500 for the erection of a boathouse; 1918, $5,252.54; 1924, $7,670.55; 1926, $11,412.87. I also asked this question:
Did the government receive the following resolution passed by the Pelee park patrons on July 21, 1926:
"That we call the attention of the Department of Marine and Fisheries to the fact that though the tug Peter Pan 2nd was in distress and blowing continuously on the morning of January 21st, a short distance from the Point

Pelee life-saving station, no effort was made by the crew stationed there to reach her until after six in the morning, and then owing to inefficiency they were unable to do so in weather so moderate that all the fishermen were attending their nets as usual; and we ask that this matter be investigated at once to prevent another such accident as the Pelee Island mishap of a year ago."
The answer that was given to question No.
18	that I asked was this:
No. (Extract from a letter received from clerk of the peace, Windsor, Ont.) "Although this took place within three miles of the lifesaving station no one there knew of it, although the boat could be seen floating bottom up quite clearly from the shore and the whistle was blown hard before the boat turned turtle."
The answer I received to question No.
19	was as follows:
The coxswain in his report of the accident states: "When the man on the beach reported ship aground made ready to go out. Saw fishing vessel Flossie G. which had been lifting nets close by proceeding to assistance, so waited their report. Survivors landed by fishing boat and taken care of at station. Survivors stated no danger whistle blown-engine room whistle blown by Captain-two short blasts."
Captain Demers in summing up his evidence of investigation states:	"Even if the lifeboat
had been manned it could not have rendered any help as the turning over of the vessel was so sudden that the crew was trapped and perished within a few minutes. The distance from the station to the place of casualty is estimated to be three miles, and when the crew searched the place on the following morning, Sunday, May 3rd, ^ when the weather and wind had subsided, this distance was covered in one hour and ten minutes. In view of this, I am of the opinion that the life-saving crew would not have rendered help and saved other lives."
Then, Mr. Chairman, I asked:
Did the government receive the resolution dated July 21, 1926?
The answer given me was:
The department contemplates a complete reorganization of this station.
I want to know from the minister:-what steps have been taken to reorganize the Point Pelee life-saving station; who is going to be put in charge of it; and what kind of service does the minister propose this station shall render to shipping in general?

Mr. Chairman, according to the information in the department from our officers, this station is operated properly and satisfactorily. As to having a reorganization towards efficiency, I need not say that we are always striving to get the best results obtainable on the part of our employees. If necessary, I am quite ready to make further inquiries and to remedy any evil which an investigation might disclose.

Supply-Marine and Fisheries

I think the minister and his officials agree that this station was no<t properly operated a year ago, otherwise they would never have given me the answer that the department contemplated a complete reorganization of the station. What did they mean by that? They simply meant that the station was not properly operated and that they proposed to reorganize) it frlom the ground up. I desire to know if the station is going to be operated properly and properly manned. It is not at the present time, and was not a year ago.

I think the word "reorganization" which has been applied to the Point Pelee station applies to all our life-saving stations. We contemplate improving the conditions everywhere. We are trying to get the best results obtainable from this and all our other life-saving stations.
Who is the coxswain at the Point Pelee life-saving station?
Unforunately I have not the name.

I do not expect the minister to have all these details in his mind, but I should like to know what was meant by "reorganization". I believe this life-saving station should be completely reorganized and re-manned.
That may be the case.
Then will the minister in the near future take steps to inquire thoroughly into the operation of this life-saving station?
Certainly.
Thank you.

Mr. Chairman, I should not like this discussion to close with the implication of the hon. member for Toronto Northwest (Mr. Church) that those of us representing constituencies on the great lakes have not taken an interest in navigation. I do not think there is any member in the house more familiar with navigation conditions on the upper lakes than I am. The acting leader of the opposition (Mr. Guthrie) Observed that he did not believe in any unwarranted expenditure. That is where he is entirely wrong. This expenditure for lifesaving stations must remain as it is, or it must be extremely large. There is no use in the member for Toronto Northwest criticizing the government for what he thinks is the inadequacy of this vote. The vote has been drifting along at about the same amount
under several governments, but every government has been increasing the appropriation each year for aids to navigation. Every man who knows the class of boats engaged in the grain trade-and my hon. friend from Toronto Northwest professes a great interest in the grain trade-knows that these boats follow each other down the centre of lake Huron, and could not be quickly reached1 by any lifesaving station located on the shores of the lake. True, we have bad storms, but no man can say at what point on the shore, either Canadian or American, a big vessel will land if she loses her rudder or propeller and gets off her course. To thoroughly patrol the Canadian side of the great lakes would mean a tremendous expenditure on life-saving stations and powerful tugs standing by the whole season long ready to respond to any emergency.
Now, when do the accidents occur to the grain boats? Never in the summer. Not until late in the fall when the navigators are anxious to make the last trip against the storm signals set by the Marine department and against the advice of more cautious men. I have known sea captains to pay high insurance rates and take chances against the storm signals puit up by the Marine department. Under those conditions there is no possibility of a life-saving crew reaching a boat in the night in zero weather and in a blinding snowstorm. No patrolling boat could give relief under those conditions. Personally I feel that the small life-saving stations on lake Huron are doing good work. I have seen volunteer crews in action from my home town and from Goderich and Southampton, and they have performed very fine services in life-saving. These small stations do very valuable work, but once a large grain boat gets adrift in bad weather, not even a large life-saving station could help her.
With regard to the marine men in the various ports, I think almost without exception the captains of fishing and towing tugs at Midland, Owen Sound, Southampton, Kincardine and Goderich have always stood by ready to render all the service they could in case of a wreck. I do not speak of lake Erie as I am not so familiar with it. But the committee has to consider not an increase of, say, one hundred thousand dollars. It has to consider one of two things: whether to continue the small life-saving stations and leave to the installation of wireless on all the boats, storm signals, and so forth, the protection of the large vessels; or whether to install sufficient stations with the necessary equipment and boats, which expenditure will

Supply-Marine and Fisheries
run into millions of dollars. It is absolutely unfair for the member for Toronto Northwest to say that this government is doing nothing to protect the lives of the sailors on the great lakes. The government is doing what the past three or four governments have done-it is spending more money every year to protect those men.

Mr. Chairman, I desire to express my entire sympathy with the object aimed at by the member for Toronto Northwest (Mr. Church) to improve our means for life-saving on the great lakes. I agree with some of the remarks made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Malcolm) that a good deal of the loss of life occurs after the ordinary navigation period closes in the fall. I suggest to the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Cardin) that he might well consider calling a conference between the ship owners, the Lake Carriers Association and the lake captains to formulate a plan for lessening the loss of life in the last few weeks of navigation between, say, the 1st and 15th of December, and sometimes later in the month. I do not wish to make the statement frequently heard on the street, that there is too much hazard taken with the lives of these men. I do not -wish to condemn the steamship companies; I have no desire to be put in that position. But I do believe that something should be done in co-operation with all these different bodies, the steamship owners, the insurance people, the Lake Carriers' Association, the captains and the men. After all it is the captains and the men who lose their lives. The insurance companies may lose a little insurance, but it is the men and the captains who suffer the loss of life. They suffer as the result of chances taken, whether under orders from headquarters or not, I do not know. At any rate I suggest that a conference might be held. The minister might consider the question of holding such a conference with the object of either shortening by law the number of days or seeing whether some other method might not be worked out whereby the loss of life could be lessened. I do not wish to suggest what should be done, because I am not an expert. But having lived all my life at the head of the lakes, where a large proportion of the shipping is carried on, I know that there is a feeling that something should be done to lessen this hazard to the lives of the seamen.

The very suggestion my
hon. friend makes is contemplated by the technical men of the department, and in the notes they have handed to me cognizance is taken of it.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Shall the hon. member have leave to withdraw his amendment? Carried.
Amendment (Mr. Church) withdrawn.

I wish to transfer the debate
now to the Pacific coast, but before proceeding to what I have to say I desire to acknowledge gratefully the fact that the department expended a good deal of money last year in certain very much needed repairs to the two life saving stations on the west coast. This will undoubtedly lead to a greater efficiency in the service.
I wish to put in a plea for better pay for these men who man the small lifeboats. In my opinon they have both a moral and a legal claim. As regards the moral claim- or, if you will, the claim of necessity-I would suggest that these men are not being paid a sufficient salary. Their salary is $65 a month, and $65 a month in British Columbia, especially in the remote parts, bulks very small as compared with the same sum in Quebec; not that we have higher standards of living, but our expenses are higher. It is true they also receive a board allowance of $25 a month, but that and more than that goes in their living expenses, because of course they must live at the station. For a single man this may not appear so unreasonable because he gets board, lodging and $65 a month. In the case of a married man, however, it is very inadequate. We presume that it is the desire of the government to stimulate immigration, and you cannot get better immigration than that which comes by way of the stork. I contend therefore that we should not discriminate against married men in the employ of the government, but should rather encourage them. Lest I be accused of putting forward a merely hypothetical case, I desire to cite two actual cases within my knowledge; one is that of a man with a wife and five children and the other a man who has a wife and a family of four. These men must maintain private homes, pay rent, and provide fuel, clothing and all other expenses involved in the upkeep of a family; the only exception is that their own actual food is provided. These places are remote. Suppose one of these men with a family of four or five-is expecting an addition to his family. He lives in a remote district and by the time the woman goes to the hospital, 100 or 150 miles away, the expenses will run up considerably. Some help has to be hired to look after the children while she is away because the husband is away at work day and night. When the bills for the hospital, the doctor and so forth are also paid that means very nearly $500; one is quite safe, at any rate, in putting

Supply-Marine and Fisheries
it at $400. I want to ask hon. members this question: By what method can a man receiving $65 a month pay house rent and provide clothing, fuel, food and so forth for a wife and four children and lay aside a sum of approximately $40 a month against future arrivals? Sixty-five dollars a month does not provide very much in the way of savings for that or any other unforeseen contingency.
It has been suggested that if the pay cannot be increased the department might at least encourage these married men iby building small houses for them; that would represent in some measure an increase in their remuneration. I might quote one sentence from a letter I have received on this subject-not from one of these men, because it is not they only who are complaining. This letter comes from an outsider with no interest in the matter other than that of a good citizen. He concludes his letter thus:
Canada requires good citizens and in my opinion the best will be those born in Canada of healthy parents who have passed the acid test of Canada citizenship.
He might have said Canadian pioneering as well.
The foregoing is an example and there must be thousands more and they cannot exist on a cup of rice per diem.
So much for the moral side of the question. Now I turn to the legal phase of it. Perhaps it is not legal, but it is very nearly so. I suggest that these men should have received the $10 increase voted by the House of Commons last year. In the supplementary estimates of last year vote 535 read:
To provide for flat increases to the civil service both inside and outside.
And the sum voted was $2,700,000. I understand that the increase was determined this way. The government asked the Civil Service Commission to submit an estimate of the amount required to provide a $10 a month flat increase to government employees with certain named exceptions. There were one or two grades to whom, in council, it was decided not to give the increase, and those grades were named. Apart from those, however, the government asked the Civil Service Commission to state how much would be required to give the whole outside and inside civil service $10 a month flat increase. The Civil Service Commision went into the matter thoroughly and finally named $2,700,000, and the money was voted by parliament
Now to anticipate the answers which I know will be given to this argument. It will be suggested that these men do not come under the Civil Service Commission. I am aware that they do not. But there are a
great many other people who got the $10 raise who did not come under the Civil Service Commission. And it never was intended either by the government, by parliament or by the Civil Service Commission that the increase should be limited to those under the commission. If it was to be limited to those under the commission why was it that the Department of Soldiers' Civil Reestablishment, and many others I could name, all received the $10 increase? .They all got it. The fact is that the money was voted for the whole civil service, inside and outside. Let me take another argument. How was the money spent? How did it reach the office holder? In the case of ordinary men coming under the commission, the civil service, at the end of the following month, after the money had been voted, made out the pay checks for $10 a month more, and that was the end of it. I inquired as to the method that was adopted with regard to those entire departments that were not under the Civil Service Commission and I was informed that what was done was this. The heads of the departments were notified that the money was available, they put in a requisition, got an order in council passed and then they paid the money out to their respective employees, those who came under that particular branch. That was all they did. There is no doubt about it; that has been done, and that is the procedure by which it was done. In cases where they came under the Civil Service Commission the commission did it; where the employees did not come under the Civil Service Commission the head of the department did it, and as far as I can see the only thing necessary in this particular case is for the head of the department concerned to put this into effect. The money is there; parliament voted it, and surely they must have intended the money to be used. It was not a lump sum voted blindly, because the Civil Service Commission presented a detailed report to the cabinet earmarking every dollar of that sum, within reasonable limits, for each department and for each branch of the different departments. There is no doubt that sufficient money was put aside to take care of these particular employees.
Then I have another bit of evidence. On the basis of the general raise which took place at that time the Civl Service Commission, either instructed by the government or on their own initiative, thought it was necessary to prepare a new classification. As everyone is aware, all employees of the gov-

Supply-Marine and Fisheries
eminent are classified. I have seen this classification and it specifically allows to this class of employees wages based on the $10 increase last year. The civil service schedule in force prior to April 1, 1927, before the $10 raise was given, gave the coxswain of a power boat from $100 to $120; that is, he began at $100 and went up to $120 by increases of $5 per month per annum. Under the new schedule prepared after April 1, 1927, and in consequence of that increase voted by parliament, this same class received from $110 to $130. So we have this anomaly, since these men have not received this increase; a new man coming into the service would start off at $110, while the man who joined up previously would only start at $100. It may be said that those who enter the service now do not get this increase, but I say they should get it, because the Civil Service Commission has so classified them. When the government is asked why this man or some other man does not get an increase we are always told that he is paid according to the schedule prepared by the Civil Service Commission, so I repeat that this is the schedule prepared by the Civil Service Commission, and I only ask that these men be paid accordingly.
Here is the matter stated concisely by the Civil Service Commission:
The amount voted by parliament last year towards salary revision is sufficiently large to cover the increases to employees not coming under the Civil Service Commission, and all that is necessary is an order in council on the recommendation of the head of the department to put the increase into effect.
That is the case in a nut shell, and all I ask is that this money be paid to these men both on the ground of necessity and justice and because it was the intention of the government that they should receive it.
I will anticipate the reply .of the minister; he will say they do not come under the Civil Service Commission, because they are in the same category as the men working on Dominion government boats, who are specifically excluded from the control of the Civil Service Commission. That is quite so, but that applies equally to the employees of the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment and several other branches of the government, and I know they received the increase. Why should not these men get it also? Surely if an increase can be justified at all it should be given to a man getting only $65 a month, and all I ask is that the increase be granted or that some plausible reason be given why it is not granted, in order that I may tell these men why they are not getting it.

there I think something could have been done at least to save the lives of those sailors. It might not have been (possible to save the boat itself, but some of the sailors might have been rescued.
May I further suggest that I think all boats plying the great lakes should be equipped with wireless. It was unfortunate that this particular boat possessed no wireless, and I think one of the conditions of operation should be that wireless must be installed on every lake-travelling boat, and there should be a wireless station at the head of the lakes in order to ensure rapid communication. I have one other small grievance to bring up; perhaps this may not be quite the appropriate item, but I think it will do. It appears that some thirteen years ago, I think in 1914, regulations were adopted by the department providing for the issuing of uniforms to the captains and some of the men on board government steamers. The custom adopted was, in the easel of boats only working for a short time each year, that they would get one suit, and, in the case of the boats working the whole year round, they would get two suits. This went on for thirteen or fourteen years, and when a man has been getting two suits a year for fourteen years he might consider, or at least anicipate, that it would continue. Apparently without any notice-I am speaking subject to correction-last October the rations, so to speak, in the shape of clothing, were discontinued. This practice was started by an order in council, and I asked the other day what order in council it was which had discontinued it, and I was told that it had been done by departmental authority. I asked the question why the remuneration of these men should be reduced in this way, and the reply I received was that the supplying of uniforms had never been regarded as remuneration. I submit that it is a very substantial part of a remuneration, the supplying of two uniforms per year. Some years ago I had occasion to write the department asking what the pay of these captains and officers was, and in the reply I received it was stated as being so much money, so much board, and uniforms, it being clearly indicated that the uniform was part of their remuneration. I think this would apply both in the opinion of him who gives and him who receives. A uniform furnished twice a year is certainly a considerable item in a man's remuneration. It may be argued that this is not direct pecuniary payment, but certainly it is an inducement to the man to go into the service and stay there.
Perhaps I did not word my question prop- ' erly, but I have not received the explanation I would like to get. It seems to me that this is a small matter with which to discontent a number of people. These men work very hard and under very trying conditions, especially during the winter time. If they had been given six months' notice, they would have had time to adjust themselves, and if they were not satisfied they could have quit the service. But it was done without any notice, and so far as the men know, and so far as I know, without any justification. I would like the minister to give us an explanation as to why this was done.

I am not in position to say positively, but I believe the regulations to which he referred are themselves confirmed by order in council, and it may be that the order in council to which he referred is one giving authority to make certain regulations.
I am not in a position to state exactly what the fact is regarding that.

I am not for the moment prepared to criticize the action of the minister in any given case, that is, from any knowledge I have of the fairness or otherwise of his action, 'but what I do criticize is the assumption by the minister- I do not say that offensively, but I cannot think of another word at the moment that will convey my meaning-of authority to determine whether this man or that man or this company or that company shall be granted a license. What I do suggest to the minister is that before taking any such action as was taken against the International Bible Students' Association in the cancellation of their license, there ought to have been formulated definite regulations controlling or directing the whole system of broadcasting. I submit to the minister that his action in cancelling that license appears to have offended a very large number of people. I am not in a position, without having before me all of the facts, to express any definite opinion whether the action taken was fair or unfair, but I do say that it has the appearance of unfairness; it has the appearances of being an arbitrary decision against this association. As far as their religious views are concerned, I am not interested in that phase of the matter at all, but I do submit that whatever their views may be, they are entitled to the right to disseminate their views unless there is some general regulations which simply takes them in along with all other persons holding various views on religious and other subjects.
My whole point, therefore, is that the action taken by the minister has the appearance of

May I quote a paragraph from the Manchester Guardian in which the new policy of the British government is commended. know that both the Liberal and the Labour
parties in England are to-day complaining about the discrimination shown by the Conservative government in the allotment of time for political addresses?

Yes, I have heard that and for a time there was real ground for that complaint. But recently there has been, I understand, a change in the regulations with regard to such matters, and it is concerning this that I wish to read the following paragraph from the Manchester Guardian:
The danger of propaganda always lies in one-sided information, in suggestion and in anonymity. As long as facts are freely disclosed there is nothing to be apprehended in open discussion of any topic. If the public always knows what individuals are speaking and proper opportunity is given to various opinions, the more controversial the subject matter of discussion the better. It is the business of the British Broadcasting Company to be impartial as between rival views, and not to heed the objections of those who think all opinions they do not like "dangerous". No subject of public importance and interest should be banned because its discussion annoys some people. If the orthodox may state their case, so may the unorthodox. If there are to be political debates, socialists should be given a hearing side by side with Liberals, and communists allowed to state their case as well as Conservatives. Many sedulously guarded myths may be dispelled by open discussion, and intelligent opinions take the place of hoary superstitions. There is no way of arriving at truth or of cultivating sound judgment except through the clash of opinion.

I am inclined to think that before very long we shall be faced in Canada with a serious situation in relation to broadcasting south of the line. That is perhaps the most dangerous feature of all. It is only a comparatively short time before these small broadcasting stations will be bought up by big American companies. I agree with the concluding remarks of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, that it is time the government brought forward something in the nature of a policy in regard to this very important question of radiotelegraphy. The only policy vhich we have to-day is one of absolute autocracy and dictatorship in regard to the use of the air for radio services. It used to be said in this country that such and such a thing was as free as the air, but in the Dominion of Canada the air is no longer free; to a very large extent it is under the direct and positive control of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries. He is an autocrat in regard to air sendee, and he is given that autocratic position or power under an act of this parliament known as the Radiotelegraph Act.

Would my hon. friend
give the reference?

It is chapter 195 of the revised statutes. Under that act, by section 4, the minister is empowered to make regulations, of which I will only read two:

(c)	defining the different kinds of licenses that may be issued, their respective forms and the several periods for which they shall continue in force;
(d)	prescribing the conditions and restrictions to which the several licenses shall respectively be subject.
Under these two subsections practically the whole control of the air of this Dominion is placed in the custody of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries. I think, for his own good and for the good of the country, at the very first opportunity he should endeavour ta lay before parliament and the country some definite policy which will considerably broaden out this matter and allow all classes in this somewhat spread-out country of ours to receive something like fair and even treatment in regard to that air which was formerly so free to everyone in this country. It is not free now, and I think in many respects the actions of the minister and of the government have been exceedingly harsh, arbitrary and autocratic, and not at all in the interests of the general body politic.
I refer, as did the last speaker, to the manner in which the Universal Radio of Canada, Limited, was dealt with by the minister or by officials of his department. This company was duly organized and incorporated with a heavy subscribed capital; it complied with all the formalities of our law and obtained from the Department of Marine and Fisheries, under the Radiotelegraph Act, a license known as a physical license for the purpose of erecting a plant and broadcasting in the Dominion of Canada. I agree that a license is only a permission, and that a man who obtains a license for a year does not have exactly a vested right in the license, although he may have a reasonable expectation that the license will be continued from year to year as long as he complies with all the requirements of the law. This Universal Radio Company subscribed its capital, erected its plant, obtained its license, complied with all the regulations of the department and started as a commercial concern in the business of radiotelegraphy. During the month of March last a most peremptory letter or notice was sent to this company, notifying them that at the end of the then current year the license would not be renewed, and giving no reasons for the refusal to renew that license. Perhaps I might read to the committee the actual letter, which is dated at Ottawa, March 8, 1928:
Sir:
You are hereby advised that private commercial broadcasting license No. 63 for the

I submit, Mr. Chairman, that such a proceeding is more than improper; courtesy demands that reasons be given under conditions of this kind.
Had the government a policy, a considered policy, nothing of this kind could arise, but here a very large amount of capital is jeopardized. This company is threatened with the loss of its whole investment, and now it transpires, since the House of Commons met, that the reason for the cancellation of this license was that through some subarrangement the International Bible Students' Association occupied some of the time at the disposal of the Universal Radio Company, and the matter broadcast by the International Bible Students' Association did not suit the opinions of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries or of someone in his department.
I desire to deny this statement the hon. gentleman is making now, and I will not permit him to make any capital out of it. All the facts and the documents are there; let him analayze those documents.

I am giving my own view and my own opinion; the minister may differ from that view and that opinion as he may see fit. Something that was being broadcast by this association did not meet with the approval of the powers that be, whether those powers were the minister himself or someone in his department. So far that is the only reason which I have been able to gather as the real cause of the difficulty, and so far as I know it is the only reason that has been
ever advanced for the refusal to renew the license of the Universal Radio Company for the current year.

I realize that many hundreds of thousands of Canadians have signed petitions, if not to this parliament, informally addressed to the Prime Minister of Canada, protesting against the action of the government and the minister in refusing to renew that license. It is a matter not of small or petty concern but of very general concern, and it looks to one who has no interest in the matter, financially or otherwise, as if the government and the minister had acted in a thoroughly autocratic and unnecessarily harsh manner in dealing with this corporation.
But the whole subject will bear some investigation. The minister or someone under him, seems to have disarranged the whole air service in and about the city of Toronto and the province of Ontario. In this disorganization and disarrangement which have taken place they seem to have been playing into the hands of their own friends. They seem to have been playing into the hands of a radio equipment in the city of Toronto which is the poorest operating in that city to-day, to the exclusion of the up-to-date installations.

I mention these things, Mr. Chairman, not because I have any direct interest in them at all, but because of the tremendous body of people in this country who are very much interested in radio. The number of listeners-in, so called, is increasing every day, and it is a serious blow to the tens of thousands of listeners-in in the province of Ontario that the most poorly equipped station, and the one which can give the poorest service, is the one that will practically control the air for full time on its circuit. Complaints are heard on every hand, and I am told that some people are obtaining special radio receiving sets of a kind that will exclude the Toronto Star's broadcast, for no other reason than that the broadcasting system of the Toronto Star is so inferior as to be practically useless in comparison with the other stations in the city of Toronto.
Surely the government will see the necessity of broadening out its policy in this matter. Surely it should take into consultation some of more representative bodies throughout the Dominion of Canada. Radio has become a commercial matter to a very large extent; boards of trade, chambers of commerce, large manufacturers, large wholesalers, they are all interested in this venture, and they are entitled to be consulted, as well as the tremendous public body which comes under the heading of listeners-in. Surely a conference of those most interested could be called, and I should think that the minister, for his own protection, would have such a conference, and a broadening out policy could be laid immediately before the parliament of Canada. If we are going to continue as we are now, we are continuing under a system which is nothing but hypocrisy pure and simple. I will grant you that parliament, when it passed the act, gave that autocratic power to the minister. We regret it now; we see the difficulty in which we have placed ourselves; but that is no reason why we should leave the act as it is or why the government should simply rest on its oars and use that arbitrary power with which parliament at one time clothed it. Radiotelegraphy is but in its infancy. It is growing every year; it is growing, one may say, every month. Next year it will be far more extensive than it is this year. It is a matter that has come to stay and to increase, and it will be worse than folly if parliament

000.

charges of graft in respect to the chartering and sale of the vessel. It is only a small boat of two or three hundred tons, and after all this discussion, if it had been a sailing boat it would have been blown off the seven seas long ago.
Item agreed to.
Ocean and river service-radio service-to provide for the general improvement of reception conditions to licensed broadcast listeners, $190,000.

I share with the Minister
of Finance the desire to expedite the business of the house, and normally I would have hesitated to make some remarks with respect to this item, but when I find that 458,026 persons, citizens of Canada, have signed a petition, addressed inadvertently to the Prime Minister of this country when it should have been addressed to the members of the House of Commons, protesting against the arbitrary manner in which the radio licenses in question had been cancelled, I think it is a subject matter for consideration by hon. members of this house.
It appears that of the 458,000 citizens who signed this petition, which has since been presented formally to the Prime Minister, making two or three cartloads, 82,468 were owners of radio sets. Why have these people registered such a vigorous protest? That is a question which enters my mind. I have taken occasion to examine the official data as well as the data supplied by the International Bible Students' Association with regard to this matter. I have no brief for the International Bible Students' Association. I am not identified with that organization in any way, and I believe that I can in a dispassionate manner, therefore, make some observations which should be pertinent to the controversy.
In my judgment there has been hasty action. Knowing the minister as I do, I cannot believe that either he or his deputy were apprised of all the facts before this arbitrary step was taken to cancel the license of this organization. I find upon examination of the official and other documents that since August, 1926, a radio license has been granted to the International Bible Students' Association; that the Universal Radio of Canada, Limited, is a commercial organization, "to sell time on the air," to use their expression. Their call letters are CJYC. They received on January 18, 1926, a license on certain terms. The terms were that that organization would build a broadcasting station some eleven miles outside the city of Toronto. In compliance with that condition of the license, that radio station was built. These licenses-they are several in number-were, according to the record I have
[Mrt Irvine.]
seen, cancelled on three weeks' notice, and practically no reasons were given for the cancellation. This organization had radio licenses almost four years ago. In November, 1924, a license was issued to them for broadcasting at Saskatoon. On April 1, 1926, licenses were issued to Edmonton and Vancouver.
Now, Mr. Chairman, it is apparent that the International Bible Students' Association, and the organization known as the Universal Radio of Canada, had been established in this country for a considerable time, recognized by governmental authorities, and granted the licenses or privileges to broadcast their ideas. I am not -contending that the views so broadcast were good, bad or indifferent; I do not know anything about them; I never heard any of their programs and I have read very little about them. But I do know that whatever they were broadcasting had the approval of the government for four years, and that when those rights were can-celled the organization, having enjoyed those privileges for four years, was not told: Now, complaints have been registered against you; come before this department and justify your broadcasting or satisfy the complaints which have been made, otherwise we will cancel your license. That course of action, I consider, would be the fair and square way to deal with the situation. I submit there is a serious responsibility upon the minister to explain why this arbitrary action was taken. The minister stated that certain complaints were made.
Now, a gentleman by the name of Walter Frederick Salter, whom I happen to have known for over sixteen years, and whose integrity and standing are beyond reproach to my personal knowledge, has made a statutory declaration dealing with this question. He is the vice-president and general manager of the International Bible Students' Association of Canada. The minister will recall that he tabled a return of the correspondence that had passed between the Department of Marine and Fisheries and certain people throughout the country. Mr. Salter in his declaration, which was sworn to on May 12, 1928, declares in paragraph 2:
I have examined carefully the correspondence tabled by the Department of Marine and Fisheries in the House of Commons in response to the request for said correspondence by J. S. Woodsworth, member of parliament for North Centre Winnipeg; on behalf of A. A. Heaps, member of parliament for North Winnipeg, and find the letters of divisional radio inspector S. J. Ellis of Toronto contain statements which I declare are incorrect, viz.:
(a) That we employed 100 returned soldiers to canvass for names to the petition of protest. The fact is that we did not employ any

one; that all the work was done freely and voluntarily by workers throughout Canada, some of whom were members of our association; some of whom were citizens indignant at the action of the government; and some of whom were returned soldiers, but the number of returned men working in Toronto could not at the outside number more than half a dozen. Then he answers several other accusations and reviews the nature of the complaints, and in paragraph 3 declares;
Considerable of the correspondence-
That is, in the return.
-refers to the activities of the said association prior to the issuance of radio broadcasting licenses and is therefore not relevant; three items refer to Vancouver, five to Edmonton, six to Saskatoon, and the balance of the correspondence to Toronto, which may be divided as follows:
(a) as to programs, 14;	(b) interference,
44; (c) miscellaneous, 22.
So you will find from tlhese facts, Mr. Chairman, and from the further analysis which is made of the correspondence, that the objections are comparatively few in number. On the other hand, when the license was cancelled it will be observed that over twenty thousand letters expressing appreciation of the programs were forwarded to the Department of Marine and Fisheries and duly acknowledged. Then large meetings were held in various parts of the country.
Now, I shall be interested in learning from the minister why these licenses were cancelled without the parties directly concerned being given an opportunity of modifying their programs, shortening their wave length or reducing the time; in other words, why were they not allowed to do something to meet the objections raised, or why were not some means suggested by which they could satisfy those objections? The fact is, as I have stated, no opportunity was afforded them. Arbitrarily the department wiped them off the air and thus deprived nearly half a million people of the right of listening to programs which they claim they enjoyed.
